$comment: P1-B1/P1-B2 (RWF-041) -- the decomposition of the `frontend` row
above into the specific modeling gap behind each occurrence.
TWO COUNTS PER SUBTYPE, AND THEY ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE:
`occurrences` is GRAPH-WIDE -- every unresolved edge anywhere the
graph builder walked, across all 17 projects. It describes the
shape of real JavaScript, and it is NOT a work queue.
`blocking` is the subset a reachability search for a real
vulnerable target actually traversed, i.e. the occurrences that
cost a verdict. In this corpus every one of them comes from ONE
case (RWB-05), so the blocking column has a sample size of one
project and must not be read as a ranking on its own.
The two columns rank the subtypes DIFFERENTLY. That disagreement
is the single most useful thing in this table.
`distinctContainingFunctions` IS NOT A CALL-SITE COUNT. A call-graph
diagnostic names the graph node an unresolved edge departs FROM --
the enclosing function -- so one node carries one entry per
unresolved call inside it (`qs/lib/stringify.js#stringify@58:17`
alone carries 17). The number of distinct CALL SITES is not
recoverable from this data and is nowhere claimed. Corrected after
independent audit; the values themselves did not change.

bySubtype.example: `stack.set(k, v)` — the receiver is a name whose value was never traced.
`isArray(x)`, `new Ctor(o)` — a bare name bound to no declaration the binder reads.
`/re/.exec(v)`, `[a, b].join('|')` — value known, members not modeled.
`funcs[index].apply(...)` — the receiver came out of an unread index.
`(function () {})()`, `f()()` — the callee is not a name at all.
`(value || '').trim()` — receiver produced by an unevaluated operator.
The generic token, kept so an unmeasured or future construct fails safe. Zero in this corpus.
